stem: A 6-month-old boy is evaluated in the clinic due to delayed motor development.  The mother reports that the boy is weaker than other children his age.  He can barely lift his head up when prone and is unable to roll to the side.  Physical examination shows generalized hypotonia and decreased deep tendon reflexes.  Further evaluation reveals a mutation in a gene encoding a protein involved in the assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs).  This patient most likely has impaired function of which of the following cellular elements?​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​
explanation:
This patient has a mutation affecting the assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), complexes composed of noncoding small nuclear RNA (snRNA) and associated proteins.  snRNPs are major components of the spliceosome, the ribonucleoprotein complex responsible for pre-mRNA splicing.  Therefore, defective snRNP assembly can impair spliceosome function.

Normally, spliceosomes remove introns from pre-mRNA and join the remaining exons to form mature mRNA.  This process depends on recognition of specific splice sites at the intron-exon boundaries.  Defective spliceosome function can cause abnormal mRNA processing, leading to inappropriate retention of introns or loss of exons and production of abnormal proteins.

In this case, the patient likely has spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.  SMN protein is required for assembly of snRNPs, which participate in pre-mRNA processing.  SMN deficiency impairs snRNP biogenesis and leads to progressive degeneration of anterior horn cells, producing lower motor neuron findings such as hypotonia, weakness, and decreased deep tendon reflexes.

(Choice A)  Eukaryotic chromatin is composed of repeated subunits called nucleosomes, which consist of double-stranded DNA wrapped around histone protein cores.  Their composition and function are not related to snRNPs.

(Choice B)  Peroxisomes are cytoplasmic organelles involved in the oxidation of very-long-chain and branched-chain fatty acids along with degradation of hydrogen peroxide.  They are not involved in snRNP assembly.

(Choice C)  Proteasomes are protein complexes that are responsible for degradation of proteins tagged by ubiquitin molecules.  Disorders involving the ubiquitin-proteasome system (eg, Alzheimer disease) can result in accumulation of misfolded proteins.

(Choice D)  Ribosomes are required for translation of mRNA into protein and comprise rRNA and ribosomal proteins, not snRNPs.

Educational objective:Small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) are major components of the spliceosome, which removes introns from pre-mRNA and joins exons to form mature mRNA.  SMN protein is required for snRNP assembly; pathogenic variants in SMN1 cause spinal muscular atrophy, characterized by degeneration of lower motor neurons with weakness, hypotonia, and decreased deep tendon reflexes.​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​
